reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Middleton's Allergy
clinicalPearls: CGD is a primary phagocyte disorder in which defective NADPH oxidase prevents the respiratory burst, so neutrophils and macrophages ingest but cannot kill certain microbes
Infections are characteristically caused by catalase-positive organisms, notably Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia, Nocardia, and the mould Aspergillus
Recurrent deep-seated infections-pneumonia, lymphadenitis, liver and other abscesses, and osteomyelitis-are typical and often present in early childhood
Exuberant granuloma formation reflects dysregulated inflammation and can obstruct hollow viscera, causing gastrointestinal or genitourinary problems that mimic inflammatory bowel disease
Most cases are X-linked (gp91phox/CYBB) and therefore affect boys, with autosomal recessive forms tending to run a milder course
Diagnosis relies on tests of the oxidative burst, historically the nitroblue tetrazolium test and now the more quantitative dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow-cytometric assay, with genetic confirmation
Long-term prophylaxis against bacteria and fungi plus interferon-gamma reduces serious infections, and prompt aggressive treatment of intercurrent infection is essential
Invasive aspergillosis and other fungal infections are leading causes of death, so a high index of suspicion and early antifungal therapy are important
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is the established curative option, and gene therapy is an evolving approach
reference.pathophysiology: CGD is caused by mutations in any of the subunits of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex (gp91phox, p22phox, p47phox, p67phox, p40phox). This enzyme normally generates superoxide and downstream reactive oxygen species that drive the microbicidal respiratory burst within the phagosome. Without a functional oxidase, phagocytes engulf organisms but fail to kill catalase-positive microbes that can neutralise their own hydrogen peroxide. Persistence of viable organisms and impaired resolution of inflammation lead to chronic granuloma formation and tissue damage. The most common form is X-linked (CYBB), with autosomal recessive forms accounting for the remainder.
additionalDifferentials: Other primary immunodeficiencies with recurrent infection (e.g. leukocyte adhesion deficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome)
Inflammatory bowel disease (granulomatous colitis can mimic Crohn disease)
Mycobacterial infection and Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease
Cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis with recurrent pulmonary infection
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causing a CGD-like oxidative defect
additionalInvestigations: Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow-cytometric assay of the neutrophil oxidative burst
Nitroblue tetrazolium test where DHR is unavailable
Genetic testing to identify the affected oxidase subunit and inheritance pattern
Microbiologic sampling and culture of infected sites, including for fungi and Nocardia
Cross-sectional imaging to localise deep abscesses and granulomatous complications
Carrier testing and genetic counselling for family members
redFlags: Invasive fungal infection, particularly aspergillosis, with respiratory or systemic decline
Deep abscess, sepsis, or rapidly progressive pneumonia requiring urgent intervention
Bowel or urinary obstruction from granulomatous inflammation
Infection with Burkholderia or Nocardia signalling severe, potentially fatal disease
reference.prognosis: Prophylactic antibacterial and antifungal therapy with interferon-gamma has substantially improved survival, though serious infections and inflammatory complications still occur. Invasive fungal disease remains a leading cause of death. Haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation can be curative, especially with well-matched donors performed before major organ damage.
pitfalls: Underestimating fungal risk and delaying antifungal therapy in a febrile CGD patient
Mistaking granulomatous colitis for ordinary inflammatory bowel disease and missing the underlying immunodeficiency
Stopping antimicrobial and antifungal prophylaxis during periods of apparent wellness
Failing to pursue genetic diagnosis, carrier testing, and consideration of curative transplantation
management: Lifelong antibacterial prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole and antifungal prophylaxis with itraconazole against catalase-positive organisms
Interferon-gamma immunomodulation to reduce the frequency of serious infection
Aggressive, prolonged, culture-directed treatment of intercurrent infections, including antifungal therapy for invasive Aspergillus and surgical drainage of abscesses
Corticosteroids for obstructive granulomatous and inflammatory complications, such as gastrointestinal or genitourinary involvement mimicking inflammatory bowel disease
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation as the curative option, with gene therapy an emerging approach
Immunology specialist follow-up with cross-sectional imaging surveillance for deep-seated infection
Genetic counselling and carrier testing for family members, given predominantly X-linked and less commonly autosomal recessive inheritance
